summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would remove time limits from targeted Indigenous education funding agreements so the Minister could contract with education providers for 2014 and later years.

It would broaden the definition of a funding year and remove old special appropriations as payments outside ABSTUDY, an Indigenous study assistance program, shifted to annual parliamentary appropriations.
The standing appropriation for ABSTUDY would remain, while obsolete provisions for earlier funding periods and the separation of appropriation provisions would be removed.
changes: The agreement provision would no longer refer only to payments during the 2001 to 2014 calendar years.
A funding year would mean 2001 or any later calendar year.
A statutory note would identify annual Appropriation Acts as the funding source for other education payments.
summary.affected: Indigenous students, education service providers and other bodies or people entering funding agreements with the Minister are affected.

speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to introduce and present the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2013, which amends the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Act 2000, and the bill was read a first time.

speeches.speaker: Nigel Scullion
speeches.brief: The Minister for Indigenous Affairs tabled a bill to amend the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Act 2000, changing its funding mechanism from special to annual appropriation for greater transparency and allowing new funding agreements from 1 January 2014 to boost school attendance for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.

speeches.speaker: Alan Tudge
speeches.brief: Introduced the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2013, which changes targeted Indigenous education funding from a special to an annual appropriation from 1 January 2014, following a 2013 to 2014 budget decision, to improve transparency and accountability.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, said the Commonwealth's Stronger Futures package funded 200 additional teachers and more than 100 teacher-housing units in the bush, but criticised the Northern Territory government for withdrawing $250 million from education over the forward estimates including $50 million next year, and said before 2001 no Aboriginal community in the Northern Territory had a school offering year 11 or 12.

speeches.speaker: Sharman Stone
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, said 58 Indigenous students were enrolled in year 7 in Shepparton in 2010 but none remained by year 12, said 34.1 per cent of Indigenous people aged 15 and over reported year 9 or below as their highest level of schooling compared with 16 per cent of non-Indigenous people, and praised the 17-year-old Ganbina mentoring program for its outcomes despite ongoing gaps between teacher expectations and results.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, said the former Labor government invested more than $5.5 billion through the Closing the Gap framework since 2008, said the School Nutrition Program provided 2,972 breakfasts and 5,419 lunches daily to 67 Northern Territory schools between January and June 2013, and said year 3 Indigenous reading proficiency rose to 74.2 per cent in 2012 from 68.3 per cent in 2008, while numeracy proficiency fell to 72.7 per cent from 78.6 per cent over the same period.

speeches.speaker: Ken Wyatt
speeches.brief: Supported the bill for providing funding certainty to schools, citing a 2006 survey led by Fiona Stanley of 4,000 Aboriginal children and families in Western Australia that found a lack of continuity in program funding undermined educational attainment, and named Western Australian schools with large Aboriginal enrolments that would benefit from the change.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Supported the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill, highlighting Richardson Primary School's adult literacy program for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander parents and the Canberra-based Australian Indigenous Leadership Centre, whose graduates saw an average income increase of $13,877 after completing its courses.
